article_title: Integrating Generative AI into Cybersecurity Education: A Study of OCR and Multimodal LLM-Assisted Instruction
citation: Patel, K., Lin, Y.-Z., Raul, G., Shih, B. P.-J., Redondo, M. W., Latibari, B. S., Pacheco, J., Salehi, S., & Satam, P. (2025). Integrating Generative AI into Cybersecurity Education: A Study of OCR and Multimodal LLM-assisted Instruction. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.02998
title: Use a lightweight OCR-to-LLM pipeline rather than multimodal LLMs to add generative AI instruction to legacy educational platforms
description: The article argues that extracting slide text with OCR and submitting it to a general-purpose LLM in a zero-shot setting is a practical, cost-effective pathway for adding generative AI support to existing educational systems. Because the OCR pipeline "offers a practical and scalable solution to bring modern LLM-based support to existing educational platforms", platforms with structured content slides can gain adaptive explanations with minimal modification to infrastructure, without resource-intensive multimodal architectures.
requirements: Instructional content already exists as structured slides
An OCR tool and LLM API access
constraints: Multimodal LLMs retain advantages for slides rich in visual content; the OCR route is best where visual context is not essential to understanding
target_learners: students in technical higher-education courses using legacy lab platforms
target_learning_goals: real-time simplification of complex technical instructional content
examples: The CLaaS platform implemented the OCR pipeline in production and collected student feedback on its output
key_sources: Patel, K., Lin, Y.-Z., Raul, G., Shih, B. P.-J., Redondo, M. W., Latibari, B. S., Pacheco, J., Salehi, S., & Satam, P. (2025). Integrating Generative AI into Cybersecurity Education: A Study of OCR and Multimodal LLM-assisted Instruction. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.02998

article_title: Know When to Trust: Making AI Scoring More Reliable for Educational Assessment
citation: Organisciak, P., & Acar, S. (2026). Know when to trust: Making AI scoring more reliable for educational assessment. Behavior Research. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-026-03058-1
title: Ocsai and confidence Python libraries for confidence-aware LLM scoring
description: The authors release two software artifacts. The ocsai library implements "confidence measurement and weighted probabilistic scoring in Python". A standalone library, named confidence, demonstrates "drop-in confidence-aware scoring for the OpenAI and Gemini APIs, as well as HuggingFace transformers, which covers many open weights models", runnable with a single command without local installation, with examples for extracting log probabilities and computing weighted scores.
requirements: Supported backend (OpenAI, Gemini, or HuggingFace transformers) for the confidence library
target_learners: researchers and practitioners scoring open-ended text responses
target_learning_goals: automated scoring of divergent thinking and other text-based measures
examples: The verbal divergent thinking implementation is available in a free web-based tool at https://openscoring.du.edu/scoringllm, shown in Fig. 8
key_sources: Organisciak, P., & Acar, S. (2026). Know when to trust: Making AI scoring more reliable for educational assessment. Behavior Research. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-026-03058-1

article_title: Medical Doctors' Offline Computer-Assisted Digital Education: Systematic Review by the Digital Health Education Collaboration.
citation: Wahabi HA, Esmaeil SA, Bahkali KH, Titi MA, Amer YS, Fayed AA, Jamal A, Zakaria N, Siddiqui AR, Semwal M, Car LT, Posadzki P, Car J. (2019). Medical Doctors' Offline Computer-Assisted Digital Education: Systematic Review by the Digital Health Education Collaboration. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/12998
title: Offline computer-based digital education (OCDE): standalone multimedia delivered via personal computer or laptop without internet or LAN connection
description: OCDE is digital education delivered through personal computers or laptops using standalone multimedia materials that require no internet or local area network connection; content is kept on magnetic or optical storage such as "floppy discs or optical storage such as CD, digital versatile disc, flash memory, multimedia cards, and external hard discs". It suits settings where internet access is absent or limited and addresses geographical, financial, and temporal barriers to face-to-face education. This review evaluated its effectiveness for medical doctors and dentists across 29 trials.
requirements: Delivered by personal computers or laptops with standalone multimedia materials without the need for internet or local area network connections
constraints: Its advantages are greatest in settings where internet access is absent or limited
target_learners: medical doctors and dentists in postgraduate training and practice
examples: Included interventions used CD-ROM software programs (19 studies), video recordings (6 studies), and multimedia (3 studies), with exposure durations ranging from 2.5 minutes to 12 months.
key_sources: Wahabi HA, Esmaeil SA, Bahkali KH, Titi MA, Amer YS, Fayed AA, Jamal A, Zakaria N, Siddiqui AR, Semwal M, Car LT, Posadzki P, Car J. (2019). Medical Doctors' Offline Computer-Assisted Digital Education: Systematic Review by the Digital Health Education Collaboration. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/12998

article_title: Findings from a Multi-Year Scale-Up Effectiveness Trial of Open-Court Reading (Imagine It!)
citation: Vaden-Kiernan, M., Borman, G., Caverly, S., Bell, N., Ruiz de Castilla, V., Sullivan, K., & Fleming, G. (2016). Findings from a Multi-Year Scale-Up Effectiveness Trial of Open-Court Reading (Imagine It!). SREE Spring 2016 Conference. https://www.sree.org
title: Multi-site cluster randomized trial with embedded implementation study of OCR at scale
description: The evaluation combined a multi-site cluster randomized trial (CRT) and an implementation study across 49 elementary schools (kindergarten through 5th grade) in 7 districts, with approximately 4,500 students and 1,200 teachers per year. Schools were "randomly assigned to treatment (N=25) and comparison (N=24)" blocking at the district level, with districts recruited over a 3-year timeframe. Year 1 focused on kindergarten and third grade cohorts; Year 2 on first and fourth grade cohorts, assessing approximately 50 students per school per cohort in fall and spring. Outcomes were measured with the GRADE and Student Motivation Form, and fidelity was captured through observations, interviews, and surveys.
requirements: District-level blocking in randomization and fall/spring pre-post assessment windows using the GRADE and Student Motivation Form
constraints: Each year of data was collected as cross-sectional and each year was analyzed independently
target_learners: elementary school students in kindergarten through 5th grade
examples: The main ITT impact analysis used a three-level model with school-level fall pretest scores on the GRADE as covariate and spring post-test scores as the dependent variable, nested within schools within districts.
key_sources: Vaden-Kiernan, M., Borman, G., Caverly, S., Bell, N., Ruiz de Castilla, V., Sullivan, K., & Fleming, G. (2016). Findings from a Multi-Year Scale-Up Effectiveness Trial of Open-Court Reading (Imagine It!). SREE Spring 2016 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED567512

article_title: Analysis of Learning Achievement and Teacher-Student Interactions in Flipped and Conventional Classrooms
citation: Sun and Wu. (2015). Analysis of Learning Achievement and Teacher–Student Interactions in Flipped and Conventional Classrooms. http://www.oeconsortium.org/about-oec/
title: OCW-integrated flipped classroom: pre-class self-study of open course materials followed by in-class collaborative group learning with TA support
description: A two-stage instructional pattern in which learners use OCW materials (instructional videos of about 30 minutes, course materials, syllabus, calendar) for self-directed pre-class study, then attend weekly 90-minute flipped sessions with small-group collaborative learning. Groups of five were mixed by prior physics knowledge, with one TA assigned to every three groups. The article states "the classroom activity chosen for this flipped classroom model was group collaborative activities, focusing on teacher-student interactions."
requirements: Learners watch the pre-class OCW videos independently before class
Sufficient TAs to provide guidance, with one TA per three groups
Heterogeneous grouping based on prior knowledge scores
constraints: The scope of the study is limited to asynchronous distance learning for the pre-class materials
target_learners: freshman university students in a compulsory physics course
target_learning_goals: physics conceptual understanding and problem solving
higher-order thinking through collaborative application of knowledge
examples: Experimental-group learners attended a 90-minute weekly flipped session with group discussions and a learning sheet assignment, plus biweekly 60-minute review sessions shared with the control group
key_sources: Sun and Wu. (2015). Analysis of Learning Achievement and Teacher–Student Interactions in Flipped and Conventional Classrooms. http://www.oeconsortium.org/about-oec/

article_title: OCRA, a Mobile Learning Prototype for Understanding Chemistry Concepts
citation: Tenku Putri Norishah Tenku Shariman and Othman Talib. (2017). OCRA, A Mobile Learning Prototype for Understanding Chemistry Concepts. 14th International Conference on Cognition and Exploratory Learning in Digital Age (CELDA 2017). https://www.worldcat.org/isbn/978-989-8533-68-5
title: OCRA: an interactive multimedia mobile learning prototype for organic reaction mechanisms
description: OCRA (Organic Chemistry Reaction Application) is a mobile learning prototype for smartphones and tablets that lets students create and visualize the mechanistic steps of organic reactions. It "uses a touch screen feature to demonstrate and conceptually visualize the mechanistic steps in an organic reaction mechanism", letting students form and break chemical bonds by sliding electrons or atoms, and covers addition, substitution, and elimination reactions. It is positioned as a supplementary tool, not a prime classroom teaching tool, and was developed based on the revised Bloom's taxonomy.
requirements: Used as a supplementary tool to learn and understand organic reaction mechanism, not as a prime classroom teaching tool
constraints: The article states it is not intended to be used as a prime teaching tool in a classroom but only as a supplementary tool
target_learners: Science Foundation Program university students taking Introduction to Chemistry
target_learning_goals: Understanding fundamental concepts of organic reaction mechanism, including addition, substitution, and elimination reactions
examples: Students tap atoms to build molecules with single, double or triple bonds, tap CHECK to verify answers, and use CLEAR ALL and NEXT buttons to move between exercises
key_sources: Tenku Putri Norishah Tenku Shariman and Othman Talib. (2017). OCRA, A Mobile Learning Prototype for Understanding Chemistry Concepts. 14th International Conference on Cognition and Exploratory Learning in Digital Age (CELDA 2017). https://www.worldcat.org/isbn/978-989-8533-68-5

article_title: Effects of online collaborative learning and simulation-based learning on pedagogical knowledge and teaching efficacy in digital education.
citation: Chang Chia-Chen, Wu Wen-Chi, Chen Li-Chu, Tsai Ping-Hsiu, Tung Chen-Yin. (2026). Effects of online collaborative learning and simulation-based learning on pedagogical knowledge and teaching efficacy in digital education. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-48620-1
title: Complementary-mechanisms account: OCL cultivates cognitive mastery, SBL reinforces performative competence
description: The article proposes that OCL and SBL affect learning through distinct but complementary mechanisms: "OCL cultivates cognitive mastery, whereas SBL reinforces performative competence and confidence through embodied practice." OCL is grounded in social constructivism, with knowledge coconstructed through social interaction, while SBL is grounded in experiential learning theory, enabling educators to practice decision-making in a safe simulated context. The account explains the divergent outcome patterns found in the study.
requirements: Effective online instruction requires integration of professional knowledge, customised learning strategies, and infrastructure for interactive discourse
constraints: The account is drawn from a quasi-experimental comparison with self-selected cohorts and no nonintervention control group
target_learners: In-service primary and secondary school teachers in digital professional development
key_sources: Chang Chia-Chen, Wu Wen-Chi, Chen Li-Chu, Tsai Ping-Hsiu, Tung Chen-Yin. (2026). Effects of online collaborative learning and simulation-based learning on pedagogical knowledge and teaching efficacy in digital education. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-48620-1

article_title: Online Learning versus Hands-On Learning of Basic Ocular Ultrasound Skills: A Randomized Controlled Non-Inferiority Trial.
citation: Kang Soo-Yeon, Yoo Jonghoon, Park Sookyung, Jo Ik-Joon, Kim Seonwoo, Cho Hyun, Lee Guntak, Park Jong-Eun, Kim Taerim, Lee Se-Uk, Hwang Sung-Yeon, Cha Won-Chul, Shin Tae-Gun, Yoon Hee. (2022). Online Learning versus Hands-On Learning of Basic Ocular Ultrasound Skills: A Randomized Controlled Non-Inferiority Trial. Medicina. https://doi.org/10.3390/medicina58070960
title: Ocular POCUS scan protocol and 0–25 blinded scoring rubric for novice training and assessment
description: The article describes a protocoled ocular POCUS scanning procedure and an expert scoring sheet used both as training content and as the outcome measure. Participants "began by selecting a predesignated ocular preset and adjusting the depth and gain", then scanned transverse and sagittal views and ONSD. Two blinded EM faculty scored settings and each basic view 0–3 and ONSD measurement 0–4, so that "Each ocular scan received a maximum of 25 points". The protocol and scoring system were based on a literature review but not validated in other settings.
requirements: Requires a pre-distributed scan protocol, a predesignated ocular preset, and expert-defined reference ONSD values
constraints: The learning material, scan protocol, and scoring system have not been validated in various settings and populations, although they were based on a review of literature
target_learners: Emergency medicine residents and interns with no prior ocular ultrasound training
target_learning_goals: Performing basic ocular point-of-care ultrasound scans and measuring optic nerve sheath diameter
examples: Used as the training protocol and outcome rubric in the randomized non-inferiority trial with four sequentially scanned eyes of two standardized patients
key_sources: Kang Soo-Yeon, Yoo Jonghoon, Park Sookyung, Jo Ik-Joon, Kim Seonwoo, Cho Hyun, Lee Guntak, Park Jong-Eun, Kim Taerim, Lee Se-Uk, Hwang Sung-Yeon, Cha Won-Chul, Shin Tae-Gun, Yoon Hee. (2022). Online Learning versus Hands-On Learning of Basic Ocular Ultrasound Skills: A Randomized Controlled Non-Inferiority Trial. Medicina. https://doi.org/10.3390/medicina58070960
